transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Lily Zhang (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (AstraHead of ML), Tom Reynolds (Astra SRE), Lena Ortiz (Astra CTO)

Summary (auto): quick review of benchmark CSVs, discuss tuning (batching, quantize, kv cache), decide next steps for production load test and pricing.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll dive straight in to the numbers — ethan you want to kick off with the p95/p99?
[00:08] Ethan: yeah sure, so we ran the 2k token scenario both with and without prefix caching, baseline provider is the one you gave us, the vendor runs with model-v1-fp16. Our Dedicated run used q4f16 with kv-cache on and continuous batching. For the single-host microbench, baseline sustained about 420 qps for 128-token average but tail latency was higher on longer prompts.
[00:28] Priya: can you clarify qps 420 for 128 tokens — our target in prod is more like 30 qps with 2k tokens, so tail behavior matters more to us than small token qps.
[00:37] Ethan: totally, for your 2k token test we see p50 ~ 900ms, p95 ~ 2.8s, p99 ~ 4.6s on Redwood Dedicated with batching set to adaptive; baseline provider p50 is similar-ish but p95 and p99 were about 15-20% higher — baseline p99 was closer to 5.4-5.7s in our runs.
[01:02] Tom: those numbers look promising, but the raw throughput you quoted earlier for baseline at 420 qps worries me — is that with batching disabled? we need to be careful comparing apples to oranges.
[01:12] Ethan: good point; baseline run I referenced was a small sequence-length run with their default batching. For the 2k sequence we ran both with batch sizes up to 8, Redwood's continuous batching plus kv-cache seems to reduce per-token compute by about 12-18% for your prompt mix. There is some variance depending on model parallel/IO saturation.
[01:35] Lena: we had a spike in memory during the q4 runs in our labs and we worry about OOM. How stable is q4f16 on GPUs you're using?
[01:42] Ethan: q4f16 is generally stable but it's model dependent; our engine has a fallback to a higher-precision kernel if we detect instability, that's why we suggested testing on your exact model artifact. Also note quantization can affect output quality slightly — in our evals we saw a small delta in rouge/semantic similarity on a couple prompts.
[02:00] Priya: what about batching latency tradeoffs? our app needs sub-3s p95 ideally.
[02:05] Maya: so two levers — reduce batch window size to lower headroom but it'll increase cost, or use prefix/KV cache aggressively which reduces decode work. For Astra's user flows where prefix is repeated, caching often buys you the most late tail reductions.
[02:22] Tom: can you remind us how the KV cache hit rate was measured? we want to make sure the numbers match our traffic pattern which is fairly heterogeneous.
[02:30] Ethan: we instrumented with a synthetic mix from the prompts you provided — about 42% of prefixes repeat within the session window which gave us an effective cache hit of ~35% in steady state. If your real traffic has lower repetition, gains shrink.
[02:48] Priya: ok that makes sense. On the baseline side, they reported slightly higher sustained throughput in single-host tests; are they using more aggressive packing or different instance types?
[02:58] Ethan: they appear to be using A100 80GB with a different operator stack; their default kernel favors throughput but at cost of higher memory footprint and worse tail latency. Our Dedicated config favors predictable tail.
[03:14] Maya: also important — we can route by policy so for non-critical workloads you could use baseline provider or Redwood hosted cheaper tier and failover to Dedicated for critical flows.
[03:25] Lena: about failover — how fast can you route around capacity issues? we need less than 2 minutes for session continuity.
[03:31] Ethan: we have automated fallbacks and health checks; warm standby and canary routes can be <60s for routing, but cold spin up for new Dedicated nodes is longer — that's why we recommend reserved capacity or burst pools.
[03:46] Tom: on networking/security — we need VPC peering, SAML SSO for the console, and KMS/HSM for keys. Also need audit logs for compliance.
[03:55] Maya: totally, we'll include SOC 2 + network diagram. For Private/VPC we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, and audit logs are available at token-level in the console.
[04:08] Priya: is there anything in the benchmark that suggests model quality regressions from quant? i.e. hallucination rates or semantic drift?
[04:15] Ethan: we did an automated eval suite; quality deltas were small for most prompts but on one category (long-form summarization) we saw a measurable 2-3% drop in semantic-similarity when using q4f16 vs fp16. We can run an extended eval with your real prompt set to quantify further.
[04:36] Priya: yes please, we'll share a broader eval set.
[04:40] Maya: action item — Priya to send production sample prompts and expected QPS; Ethan will run extended evals including rouge, bertscore, and p95/p99 for 2k sequences.
[04:52] Tom: for the upcoming infra test — what environment do you need from our side?
[04:57] Ethan: ideally a staging VPC peered with our test runner, basic firewall rules to allow test harness, and a window of ~2 hours at low external load. We'll provide exact IPs.
[05:10] Lily: pricing note — if you go Dedicated with reserved capacity we can tighten latency SLO and provide a committed discount; we'll draft a pricing option in the next day or so.
[05:21] Priya: any gotchas we should be aware of re: billing for burst vs reserved?
[05:25] Maya: bursts are billed at a premium rate; reserved gives the best unit economics. Also caching and batching reduce total token compute which impacts cost. We'll include sample cost-per-100k-requests in the estimate.
[05:38] Lena: competitor question — BaselineCloud told us they can do 99th percentile under 3s at our profile but we saw their p99 higher in your tests. Could that be environment/tuning?
[05:48] Ethan: yes tuning and model binary matter a lot; kernel choices and fusion can change p99. We try to match configs but sometimes vendor defaults are opaque.
[05:58] Maya: quick note on observability — console exposes per-route token-level metrics and tracer hooks you can connect to Datadog; we can also provide raw logs for the benchmark runs.
[06:09] Tom: ok good. Let's recap next steps and owners.
[06:13] Maya: recap: Ethan export + share raw perf logs and p95/p99 by 2026-08-14; Maya attach SOC2 + network diagram by 2026-08-13; Lily send pricing options by 2026-08-16; Priya send production prompt set and QPS by 2026-08-14; Tom confirm test window by 2026-08-17.
[06:35] Priya: sounds good. One more quick Q about telemetry retention — how long do you keep detailed request logs by default?
[06:42] Lily: default retention is 30 days for raw logs; we offer extended retention as an add-on.
[06:48] Priya: thanks.
[06:50] Maya: ok we'll follow up in email with attachments and schedule the load test. Thanks everyone.
[06:55] Lena: thanks all.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hears (product names sometimes transcribed as baselinecloud, baselined provider), timestamps approximate. File attachments referenced: benchmark_spreadsheet.csv (link to shared drive), SOC2_summary.pdf, staging_network_diagram.png.

End of transcript.
